UNDERSTAND that renewal is a process. Be dedicated to it:

Titus 1:7: (NASB) For the overseer must be above reproach as God's steward, not self-willed, not quick-tempered <3711>, not addicted to wine, not pugnacious (eager or quick to argue, quarrel or fight), not fond of sordid gain.

Quick-tempered: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3711 orgilos Thayer’s Green-English Lexicon: prone to anger, irascible In other words, having the tendency to be easily angered. Having a short fuse. Testy. Thin-skinned, touchy, crotchety, people have to walk on eggshells around you. Overly sensitive to offenses or criticism. Does this ever sound like us?

Every minister of Christ is not perfect in all these things, but they need to be growing in that development. We should be dedicated to this renewal process.

Replace your SINFUL DESIRES with a Christlike heart:

Colossians 3:12-13: (NASB) 12So, as those who have been chosen of God, holy and beloved, put on a heart of compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness and patience; 13bearing with one another, and forgiving each other, whoever has a complaint against anyone; just as the Lord forgave you, so also should you.

There is not a lot of room for anger or anything negative if our hearts are full as described.

REALIZE that simple irritability can blind you to true godliness:

John 7:23: (NASB) If a man receives circumcision on the Sabbath so that the Law of Moses will not be broken, are you angry <5520> with me because I made an entire man well on the Sabbath?

Angry: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #5520 cholao; from #5521; to be bilious, i.e. (by implication) irritable (enraged, "choleric") This word means to be spiteful or irritable. In other words, Jesus is saying: I just healed him, and you are going to be irritated with me? The Pharisees were blinded to the goodness of the miracle because they were irritable at Jesus telling them they were doing wrong. Irritability can be a blinding factor in our Christian walk. We of all people have everything to be joyful about

because we know the plan of God and walk by His grace through His son. We have to recognize when we get irritable and do what we can to turn it around. Get mad, then get over it. ― Colin Powell Easy to memorize – hard to apply!

Replace your BROKEN REACTIONS with love and peace – fill the void:

Colossians 3:14-15: (NASB) 14Beyond all these things put on love, which is the perfect bond of unity. 15Let the peace of Christ rule in your hearts, to which indeed you were called in one body; and be thankful.

This is agape love – the selfless kind of love that is not expecting anything in return. This process brings us to this special kind of love that goes beyond our natural human reactions.

SEEK OUT godly responses when anger begins to swell:

James 1:19-20, 22: (NASB) 19…But everyone must be quick to hear, slow to speak and slow to anger <3709>; 20for the anger <3709> of man does not achieve the righteousness of God. 22But prove yourselves doers of the word, and not merely hearers who delude themselves.

The anger of man does not achieve the righteousness of God – this is good to memorize!

The anger we feel is most likely the anger of man, so face it, focus and develop what is necessary to replace this anger.

Allow CHRIST’S WORD to dwell in you and MIRROR JESUS:

Colossians 3:16-17: (NASB) 16Let the word of Christ richly dwell within you, with all wisdom teaching and admonishing one another with psalms and hymns and spiritual songs, singing with thankfulness in your hearts to God. 17Whatever you do in word or deed, do all in the name of the Lord Jesus, giving thanks through him to God the Father.

This is not just an emotional encouragement, singing hymns together. This comes at the end of all the Christian growth of the church at Colossae. It is the epitome of what we have become. We reach this stage in the process by maturity, not emotion.

CHOOSE the leadings of God’s spirit over those of your own spirit:

Ephesians 4:30-32: (NASB) 30Do not grieve the holy spirit of God, by whom you were sealed for the day of redemption. 31Let all bitterness and wrath <2372> and anger <3709> and clamor and slander be put away from you, along with all malice. 32Be kind to one another, tender- hearted, forgiving each other, just as God in Christ also has forgiven you.

Wrath <2372> here is that “bad wrath” word – an outburst of rage.

We want to choose the leadings of God’s spirit over our own. We may have an anger problem, but it is not an excuse. It needs to be dealt with in a Christ- like way. For those with a big problem with anger, we encourage you to seek professional help. It is always appropriate to seek help through counseling so that we can be God-honoring.

I am a Christian and I am angry! What now?

Pause, consider, take a breath, look at the Scriptures, get some help so that as you go through life, you can realize you are angry. Likely that anger is not righteous indignation. This may be a difficult point to get to.

We see from the example of Jesus how he never did anything to hurt anybody, but he did stop the evil. We first need to learn how to control ourselves. Follow the Scriptures, work together, strive to reach the higher standards of God’s righteousness because God’s anger is always productive. Is ours? So, I’m a Christian and I’m angry! What now?

For Jonathan, Rick, Julie and Christian Questions...

## Episode 1119 — Does the Coronavirus Fit Into God’s Plan?
Published: 2020-03-30
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/current-events/1119-coronavirus/

2 Peter 3:11: (KJV) Seeing then that all these things shall be dissolved, what manner of persons ought ye to be in all holy conversation and godliness.

Social distancing. Three months ago, if we had heard that term, we may have thought it was describing someone who was a loner or someone who swore off social media. Now we not only all know what it means, we feel its meaning and it is frightening.

I was in the grocery store today, and on the floor of the line for self-checkout there were tape lines six feet apart so shoppers could more easily avoid contact. The novel coronavirus – COVID- 19 - has arrived. It is potent, fearsome and sneaky. Because of its presence the entire world has been altered socially and economically in a matter of a few months. As Christians, what are we supposed to do with this pandemic? What should we know, how should we act, and most importantly, is this virus connected to God’s plan? Is this the “time of the end” everyone is worried about? No, but it is a piece of the puzzle that is part of the “End Times.”

We have seen a lot of Scriptures thrown around on social media lately, trying to be prophetic.

Is COVID-19 from God? Was it predicted along with other recent tragedies in the world?

Julie has done a lot of background research on COVID-19 for this podcast. What is COVID-19? (Source: https://www.cdc.gov/coronavirus/2019-ncov/downloads/2019-ncov-factsheet.pdf) What is coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19)? Coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) is a respiratory illness that can spread from person to person. The virus that causes COVID-19 is a novel coronavirus that was first identified during an investigation into an outbreak in Wuhan, China.

Viruses are infectious particles. On their own, they cannot make more of themselves, and can only be replicated with the help of a living cell. Julie: I am blessed to have a lifelong friend, Dr. Wendy Trzyna, Professor of Microbiology at Marshall University. I asked Dr. Wendy a few questions: Why is coronavirus so contagious? Dr. Wendy Trzyna, Professor of Microbiology at Marshall University - Coronavirus first attaches specifically to cells of the airway, gets into the cells and essentially reprograms these cells to make more viruses. The infected cell can produce millions of new viruses, which can then be transmitted to other people, often even before symptoms occur in the originally infected person. Since it resides in the upper respiratory tract and causes only mild or no symptoms in about 80 percent of people, many people do not even realize they are contagious. It is spread very easily by people coughing or sneezing or via their hands if they have rubbed their nose. The virus can remain infectious on some surfaces for as long as three days. It is the 20 percent who will develop severe life- threatening symptoms who are most at risk.

This is actually the seventh kind of human coronavirus we have identified: 229E, NL63, OC43, HKU1, MERS (MERS-CoV) - Middle East Respiratory Syndrome, and SARS (SARS-CoV) - Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome. The seventh is called SARS-CoV-2, the novel coronavirus or COVID-19. They are named for their crown-like spikes on their surface. We have all seen the pictures of the virus ball with those little spikes coming out of it. We asked Dr. Wendy what those are.

What are those spiky things? Dr. Wendy Trzyna, Professor of Microbiology at Marshall University - The coronavirus has spike proteins on its surface. These spike proteins are what bind to receptors on the target cell – in this case, the cells that line the respiratory tract, called epithelial cells. Think of the spike protein as a key and the receptor on the cells as the lock. This is how it attaches to our cells.

And this virus binds at least ten times more tightly to this receptor than does the spike protein of the SARS virus. Once our bodies make antibodies that are specific for the spike protein, the virus would then be prevented from binding. Scientists around the world are learning more each day about the virus, understanding its shape and the mechanisms it uses to infect and replicate in our cells. A detailed understanding of these processes will provide potential targets for therapeutic intervention and vaccine development.

We are trying to give a factual foundation of understanding in order to better cope with the panic surrounding us.

What is a pandemic? (Source: https://www.health.com/condition/infectious-diseases/epidemic-vs-pandemic) That word – pandemic - is enough to induce widespread panic, and with good reason: According to the World Health Organization, a pandemic is the worldwide spread of a new disease. "A pandemic is when an epidemic spreads between countries," says David Jones, MD, PhD, a professor of the culture of medicine at Harvard University. In the case of COVID-19 specifically, the World Health Organization said that it's the first pandemic caused by a coronavirus.

Declaring a pandemic is important because pandemic vaccines are paid for by governments, and conventional vaccines are paid for by ordinary health services. A pandemic frees up funds.

As of this broadcast, COVID-19 was in approximately 177 countries.

How it enters the body, The Coronavirus Explained & What You Should Do, Kurzgesagt – In a Nutshell - The lungs are lined with billions of epithelial cells. These are the border cells of your body lining your organs and mucosa waiting to be infected. Corona connects to a specific receptor on its victim’s membranes to inject its genetic material. The cell, ignorant of what’s happening, executes the new instructions which are pretty simple - copy and reassemble. It fills up with more and more copies of the original virus until it reaches a critical point and receives one final order - self-destruct. The cell sort of melts away, releasing new Corona particles ready to attack more cells. The number of infected cells grows exponentially. After about 10 days, millions of body cells are infected, and billions of viruses swarm the lungs.

We asked Dr. Wendy how the novel Coronavirus compares so far to other pandemics and this is what she said: How does this pandemic compare to previous pandemics? Dr. Wendy Trzyna, Professor of Microbiology at Marshall University - COVID-19 is spreading much more than either Swine flu or SARS did. This may be because of the fact that it's not as lethal as SARS, MERS or Ebola. The more lethal a virus, the less likely it becomes super infectious since it’s killing the host and thus not spreading. Swine flu, the 2009 H1N1 pandemic, was highly infectious but not very lethal. A lot of people were infected around the world, but the death rate was very low – around 0.01 – 0.02 percent. SARS was a lot deadlier but a lot less infectious; it didn't spread anywhere nearly as easily as this virus and was reasonably quickly contained. The SARS epidemic of 2003 killed around 10 percent of the 8,098 confirmed cases. COVID-19 has the worst of both. It looks like it spreads as easily as Swine flu but kills almost as many as SARS, with lethality currently at 4.5 percent globally, according to data from the Johns Hopkins Coronavirus Resource Center. As of the date we aired this podcast, globally there were 775,286 cases with 37,140 deaths, a 4.8% fatality rate. In the United States, the fatality rate was 1.8%. (Note: These numbers have since increased.)

Ebola had a 40 percent mortality rate and only affected nine countries. 180 countries are currently affected by the coronavirus.

We need to be aware but not afraid. https://informationisbeautiful.net/visualizations/COVID-19-coronavirus- infographic-datapack/ Please see page 20 of Bonus Material for infographics.

Then two kinds of cells that destroy, The Coronavirus Explained & What You Should Do, Kurzgesagt – In a Nutshell - Two kinds of cells, in particular, wreak havoc. First, neutrophils, which are great at killing stuff, including ourselves. As they arrive in their thousands, they start pumping out enzymes that destroy as many friends as enemies. The other important type of cells that go into a frenzy are Killer T cells which usually order infected cells to commit controlled suicide. Confused as they are, they start ordering healthy cells to kill themselves, too. The more and more immune cells arrive, the more damage they do and the more healthy lung tissue they kill. This might get so bad that it can cause permanent and irreversible damage that leaves to lifelong disabilities. In most cases, the immune system slowly regains control. It kills the infected cells, intercepts the viruses trying to infect new ones and cleans up the battlefield. Recovery begins.

We should always try to live up to a higher standard. In this case, apply the prescribed safety protocols and help encourage others not to be fearful.

John 16:33: (NASB) These things I have spoken to you, so that in me you may have peace. In the world you have tribulation, but take courage; I have overcome the world.”

Jesus left us a legacy of peace:

John 14:27: (NASB) Peace I leave with you; my peace I give to you; not as the world gives do I give to you. Do not let your heart be troubled, nor let it be fearful.

Let the peace of Jesus drive us to be a beacon of light.

Trish asks: Doesn’t God overrule these things for our best interest? God will not automatically put a dome over us to keep us safe if we want to break protocol and meet together. We should not step outside of using the spirit of a sound mind, using our spiritually highest motive and thinking. We do not want to hurt ourselves or others.

What does God’s plan look like? There WILL be a time of worldwide trouble:

Luke 21:25-26: (NASB) 25There will be signs in sun and moon and stars, and on the earth dismay among nations, in perplexity at the roaring of the sea and the waves, 26men fainting from fear <5401> and the expectation of the things which are coming upon the world; for the powers of the heavens will be shaken.

This sounds scary! Sea and the waves symbolically represent restless humanity. This shows a dramatic unrest. The time of trouble is a serious situation.

Matthew 24:22: (KJV) And except those days should be shortened, there should no flesh be saved: but for the elect's sake those days shall be shortened.

This sounds like bad times are ahead. We do not know what that will look like, but we are warned that the trouble of that time will be serious, recognizable and unmistakable. It will crumble the present societies.

This time will come upon the world in the same way labor pains come when a child is to be born:

1 Thessalonians 5:1-3: (NASB) 1Now as to the times and the epochs, brethren, you have no need of anything to be written to you. 2For you yourselves know full well that the day of the Lord will come just like a thief in the night. 3While they are saying, Peace and safety! then destruction will come upon them suddenly like labor pains upon a woman with child, and they will not escape.

The pain of labor may seem unbearable, but it lasts only a short moment. This coronavirus is part of the labor pains. God’s providence is bigger than the moment. It is eternal and He has it all under control. God’s grace is with us; we are not alone. We are to stay close to God through Christ regardless of what is happening.

How do we know when the end times are? Israel is a massive and obvious key to God’s timing.

We have witnessed the miraculous return of Israel to their land, yet there is more trouble to come:

Psalms 83:1-5: (NASB) 1O God, do not remain quiet; do not be silent and, O God, do not be still. 2For behold, Your enemies make an uproar, and those who hate You have exalted

themselves. 3They make shrewd plans against Your people, and conspire together against Your treasured ones. 4They have said, Come, and let us wipe them out as a nation, that the name of Israel be remembered no more. 5For they have conspired together with one mind; against You they make a covenant.

Certain prophecies about Israel still have to happen before the big trouble comes. This gives us an idea of where we are on the stream of time. For more about Israel in prophecy, please search our archives for Episode 824: What Did Jesus Say About Israel?

In spite of all their upcoming troubles, Israel eventually will be highly blessed and will bless others:

Zechariah 8:20-23: (NASB) 20Thus says the LORD of hosts, It will yet be that peoples will come, even the inhabitants of many cities. 21The inhabitants of one will go to another, saying, Let us go at once to entreat the favor of the LORD, and to seek the LORD of hosts; I will also go. 22So many peoples and mighty nations will come to seek the LORD of hosts in Jerusalem and to entreat the favor of the LORD. 23Thus says the LORD of hosts, In those days ten men from all the nations will grasp the garment of a Jew, saying, Let us go with you, for we have heard that God is with you.

This shows us the “birth” after the birth pangs. Jesus taught us to pray: Thy kingdom come, Thy will be done on earth as it is done in heaven. This has not happened yet, but Jesus told us to pray for it, so it is a done deal! Let the peace of God that passes all understanding wrap us up in the promise of what is coming so the fear that surrounds us now can be handled with grace, courage, strength and faith.

The end of all of this is a beginning!

Revelation 21:4: (KJV) And God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death, neither sorrow, nor crying, neither shall there be any more pain: for the former things are passed away.

Where we are in the panic of this pandemic is difficult and scary, but it is not the end. Make it a beginning.

Remember in the first segment, we talked about people misapplying Scripture, saying it predicted this virus? We found a text that 100 percent applies to what is going on. It tells us we definitely should be stockpiling! Matthew 6:20 (NASB) tells us to store up for yourselves treasures in heaven. You can’t take it with you, but you can send things ahead of time!

So, does the coronavirus fit into God’s plan?

For Jonathan and Rick (and Julie!) and Christian Questions... think about it!

## Episode 1317 — It’s Time to Change, but How Much Is Enough?
Published: 2024-01-22
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/character/1317-change/

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Let’s face it, we all know that each and every one of us can be better. We can be better human beings, better friends, co-workers, spouses, cousins and certainly better Christians. The challenge here is obvious. Being “better” requires change— significant change. To be better in whatever area we are focusing on requires a different mindset, which brings different words and actions. This all translates into work! So, how do we go about actually becoming “better”? Where do we start? How many parts of our lives do we try to change? Do we work on them all at once? How do we figure out what the very highest priorities are? What if we fail? How does the Bible guide us with all of these details?

Let’s begin with our highest priorities. In the book of Romans, the Apostle Paul reasons through our priorities in great detail. A very general overview of Romans shows him detailing how sinful the world is. He spends several chapters showing us how we are to be different from this world because we are called to Christ. This call goes above the Law of Moses and requires our highest loyalty.

Chapters 9 through 11 lament Israel’s rejection of Jesus and how by God’s grace, this rejection will ultimately be reversed. His point is that Israel had God’s favor, His undivided attention, and they treated it too lightly.

Paul begins chapter 12 with this dramatic example in mind:

Romans 12:1: Therefore I urge you, brethren, by the mercies of God, to present your bodies a living and holy sacrifice, acceptable to God, which is your spiritual service of worship.

In other words, look at what Israel did, and don’t do that. Don’t mess up this opportunity. Learn from the examples of what they did wrong.

The message here is clear. With the message of Israel’s failure as context, Paul is urging every Christian to live a life of true and complete sacrifice.

We often quote this verse to those newly interested in the Christian life. But this also applies to those who have been in the way for a time. This standard applies no matter how long we have been in the way.

Living like Paul admonishes requires changes to be made. But does this mean every single thing in our lives needs changing? In what areas of life should we be truly dissatisfied? Dissatisfaction can be a blessing or a curse, in that encouraging people to be dissatisfied with their spiritual maturity can easily lead to feeling depressed in our inadquacies, but that’s not the point.

Let’s suggest that change is necessary in two different categories—alteration and abandonment.

1. Change can mean alteration. We can become better. We can change by altering certain parts of our lives so they can more definitively reflect Christ in us. For example, when I began to follow Christ, I learned that some of my language was not appropriate, and I needed to alter how I spoke. That took work, as I was coming from a worldly background.

2. Change can mean abandonment. Sometimes we can only become better by abandoning certain thoughts, words or actions, and completely replacing them with spiritually-sound thoughts and responses. For this category, think about destructive behaviors like addiction, abuse, adultery and so on.

Alteration, then, means making a change as we move forward. Whereas, abandonment means totally leaving something behind—no vestiges of the behavior or thought can follow us. We aren’t secretly hiding something.

What specifically would need to be abandoned? In this next text, is the Apostle Paul really suggesting we can avoid abandoning anything? Did he give us a way to hold onto our sinful selves?

2 Corinthians 12:8–10: 8 Concerning this I implored the Lord three times that it might leave me. 9 And he has said to me, my grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness. Most gladly, therefore, I will rather boast about my weaknesses, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me. 10 Therefore I am well content with weaknesses, with insults, with distresses, with persecutions, with difficulties, for Christ's sake; for when I am weak, then I am strong. Is Paul just accepting he is weak and can’t do anything about it, so he will just be content with where he is? Is he boasting about his weakness and that the power of Christ will show itself anyway? Is he saying, God loves me just the way I am.

How is Paul “abandoning” his weaknesses?

Paul can accept the fact that he is imperfect and broken, because he has accepted the fact that Christ in him can be the overcoming factor for his brokenness. He is not accepting that broken is good! He is accepting that brokenness exists in all of us, and Christ can help us cope and work on overcoming it. There is a big difference between God loves me the way I am; I don’t need to change, and God loves me the way I am and will help me do better.

Paul tells us in chapter 5, that where there is sin, there is corresponding grace from God. He then addresses the logical question: Does that mean we can sin all we want because God will keep forgiving us?

Paul clarifies this emphatically in Romans 6:

Romans 6:1–4,6–7: 1 What shall we say then? Are we to continue in sin so that grace may increase? 2 May it never be! How shall we who died to sin still live in it? 3 Or do you not know that all of us who have been baptized into Christ Jesus have been baptized into his death? 4 Therefore we have been buried with him through baptism into death, so that as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we too might walk in newness of life. 6 knowing this, that our old self was crucified with him, in order that our body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be slaves to sin; 7 for he who has died is freed from sin.

We need to carefully examine ourselves to see what thoughts or behaviors we need to abandon. We are dead to our old lives. There should not be a connection anymore. It’s in the past. We can’t drag our old, sinful life into this new life—the two don’t work together. Knowing that there is NO room to allow sin in our lives, let’s focus in on what needs to absolutely be abandoned. This scripture helps us with perspective:

Galatians 5:19–21: 19 Now the deeds of the flesh are evident, which are: immorality, impurity, sensuality, 20 idolatry, sorcery, enmities, strife, jealousy, outbursts of anger, disputes, dissensions, factions, 21 envying, drunkenness, carousing, and things like these, of which I forewarn you, just as I have forewarned you, that those who practice such things will not inherit the kingdom of God.

Some of these seem obvious like immorality and idolatry, but jealousy? Anger? Disputes? These will keep us from inheriting the kingdom of God? Uh oh!

One warning when we start looking at the ugly parts of ourselves to determine what to completely give up: we can get so overwhelmingly negative and down on ourselves that we become paralyzed and can’t move forward. If we’re facing addictions or depression, for example, we likely need professional help, and there’s nothing wrong with that. This is a big list. It is easy to get discouraged thinking about our failings. It could be harboring jealousy, arguing with someone or even something much worse—does this mean we can’t inherit the kingdom? No, it means we don’t remain in the failing, strife, outbursts of anger and so on. We fight them.

We ask for forgiveness and help to overcome.

We step above and beyond and keep moving forward. The problem comes if we use these weaknesses as excuses for our behavior. These need to be abandoned; they need to be attacked and not tweaked or adjusted.

As we examine the following six phases of change, we want to put these things into the category of urgent work for every day. These are what we should be abandoning. How do we do that? How do we get our hearts, minds and will to move forward with the work of changing?

Don’t get stuck with dissatisfaction as an end result. This is an attention-getter to alert us. It is not an end; it is an important beginning.

It looks like the idea of change for any serious Christian is an idea that needs to be taken VERY seriously and needs to be here to stay.

As we begin our journey of change, we have touched on things that need to be abandoned. What’s the difference with things that need to be altered? There is a big difference between these two things. Something that needs altering might be a thought or behavior that is already tempered with some level of goodness and integrity. A quick example might be something like, “I do love God’s word, but I really think I need to spend more personal time studying. Let me alter my behavior to raise my focus closer to my heavenly Father in study.” This change is taking an acceptable basis and growing a better habit.

My cousin Paul just told me this story. When he was a boy, his father told him to sweep out the garage. Like any boy who really wants to play with his friends instead, he quickly swept out the garage and left for the park. He’s playing ball and looks up and sees his father signaling to him. They go back to the garage together and his dad says, “I thought I told you to sweep the garage.” “But I did! I really did!”

But there was a rug on the concrete. His dad lifted up the rug and moved it out of the garage. All kinds of little bugs crawled out, and underneath it was dusty and dirty. He handed Paul the broom. “You didn’t finish the job.”

As an adult, Paul likened what was under the rug to these changes we need to alter. You might think, well, I’m not murdering anybody or committing adultery like THOSE people! I’m fine! And yet, there’s still more we can do to be pleasing to our heavenly Father. We need to lift up the rug, see what crawls out and sweep it away.

We want to “do the work” completely the first time! Trials come and we learn the lessons. We don’t want the same trial to have to be repeated multiple times because we are just too stubborn to learn. So, we sweep the floor well the first time and keep the lesson inside our heart and mind.

Some examples of scripturally positive changes with scripturally positive beginnings—these are things that just need some altering:

2 Peter 1:5–8: 5 Now for this very reason also, applying all diligence, in your faith supply moral excellence, and in your moral excellence, knowledge, 6 and in your knowledge, self-control, and in your self-control, perseverance, and in your perseverance, godliness, 7 and in your godliness, brotherly kindness, and in your brotherly kindness, love. 8 For if these qualities are yours and are increasing, they render you neither useless nor unfruitful in the true knowledge of our Lord Jesus Christ.

There’s always something more we can add. There’s always a higher level to strive for. All diligence means “in all earnestness and haste.” This reminds us of the Apostle Paul urging us forward in Romans 12:1.

We can say, “There is always something more…” with discouragement. Or, we can look at altering or tweaking our behaviors by saying, “There is always something more I can do to grow closer to my heavenly Father. There is another step I can take to get closer.” But realistically, we’ll never get there. I will never have perfect patience. I can’t say I will never again be frustrated and react poorly. Why even try?

We ARE going to get there because it is not a matter of being perfect; it is a matter of working hard at our intentions and our actions so God can bless us. “Getting there” has to be defined, not by you or I, but by our heavenly Father. Let’s keep that in mind so there is a reason to try, and we become a more well-rounded Christian. This is following Jesus, exactly what a disciple is supposed to be doing.

We have observed dissatisfaction as a foundation for change. Because dissatisfaction is an attention getter, we must focus it on creating positive momentum. While we might start with being dissatisfied, don’t stop there. Keep moving forward.

CHANGE BEGINS WITH DESIRE: Desired change must be consistent with our highest Christian aspirations! If it’s just an intellectual thought in our head, we will be discouraged because it’s too big and an impossible goal. We have to really desire the change in our heart in order for it to have any hope of working. Where is the desire coming from? Let’s go back to our theme text:

Romans 12:2: And do not be conformed to this world, but be transformed <3339> by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what the will of God is, that which is good and acceptable and perfect.

Transformed: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3339 metamorphoo; to transform (literally or figuratively, “metamorphose”) Metamorphose: to change completely in form or nature

Your time as a caterpillar has expired. Your wings are ready! — Author unknown We must be willing—have the desire—to go through the process of changing into something different from what we were. Do we want to stay how we have been, or do we want to become more Christlike?

The #3339 above is an internal change. But there is another New Testament word for transforming, #3345, which can have a VERY different meaning, as it is focused on outward and not inward change. This word can depict a change distortion. Disguise: Strong’s Exhaustive Concordance #3345 metaschematizo; to transfigure or disguise; figuratively, to apply (by accommodation): transfer, transform (self) It looks like a change on the outside but really isn’t on the inside—it is only a superficial change. Americans use the idiom PUTTING LIPSTICK ON A PIG. Adding lipstick doesn’t change the pig. You can try to make it look more attractive, but it’s still the same pig. When we desire to change, it can be one of two ways: The desire can cause a positive change from within, #3339, OR It can get distorted and be on the outside, so we only APPEAR to have changed, #3345. I’LL PUT SOMETHING ON FROM THE OUTSIDE IN, TO LOOK THE PART THAT I CLAIM TO SEEK.

Watch for the word “disguise” in the following scripture:

2 Corinthians 11:13–15: 13 For such men are false apostles, deceitful workers, disguising <3345> themselves as apostles of Christ. 14 No wonder, for even Satan disguises <3345> himself as an angel of light. 15 Therefore it is not surprising if his servants also disguise <3345> themselves as servants of righteousness, whose end will be according to their deeds.

This is used in a negative or fake sense of changing. It's not really a transformation. Let’s say I want to be a more faithful Christian, so I will bring my Bible to church on Sunday and everyone can see I’m taking notes and am really engaged, but I live my same old sinful life Monday through Saturday. Because there is no real transformation, just the act of going to church won’t make me more faithful. It’s a good start, but there’s more work to be done.

In other words, I’m going to “look” the part, but I’m not going to “become” the part. We have to work at becoming something different, something higher; following that path to God.

Instead of a distorted change, what would a real change look like?

Romans 12:3: For through the grace given to me I say to everyone among you not to think more highly of himself than he ought to think; but to think so as to have sound judgment, as God has allotted to each a measure of faith.

What does sound judgment look like in our hearts? Hopefully, we humbly ask ourselves, Why has God called me, and how can I use my abilities and improve to please Him? There’s a subtle point here in addition to assessing ourselves in an honest way. The phrase everyone among you reminds me about the trial of comparison. I’ll never be the Apostle Paul. I’ll never even be Rick or Jonathan. And don’t even get me started on how to become more Christlike. How can I think I can be like Christ? Does God even compare us to others?

We can’t be like Christ! We will never get there in this life. However, God did not call us to become something we are not capable of becoming. He called us to fulfill the potential within ourselves. That is the whole point of the change reality. The Father knows each of us and will help us grow into a more spiritually-sound version of ourselves.

One of the biggest mistakes we make when we realize the need for change is to throw our entire self away and try to change all of it at once. It is too much. Human nature changes in steps. We need to take the steps of going from where we were, to where we are now, and then to where we will be. We need to work on the pieces one at a time. CHANGE ENGAGES WITH RECOGNITION.

Recognition of who and what we have become subservient to.

The necessary recognition for change is driven by seeking to understand and embrace my true place in reality.

I am called by God to play a role in His plan and within the brotherhood of Christ:

Romans 12:5–8: 5 so we, who are many, are one body in Christ, and individually members one of another. 6 Since we have gifts that differ according to the grace given to us, each of us is to exercise them accordingly: if prophecy, according to the proportion of his faith; 7 if service, in his serving; or he who teaches, in his teaching; 8 or he who exhorts, in his exhortation; he who gives, with liberality; he who leads, with diligence; he who shows mercy, with cheerfulness. These texts don’t build these activities one on top of another. It says one does this, one does that, one does this, one does that. It gives us permission to not be perfect, but it gives us motivation to find what we CAN do, and to do it with zeal and diligence.

We don’t all contribute in the same way. While I can’t give a sermon, I can be an example of one to those around me. I know a dear sister in Christ with extremely serious health problems that keep her housebound. But with a few clicks on the keyboard, she’s in Africa studying with other sisters. Every day, she handwrites cards of encouragement that are sent all over the world. Her service is vibrant, contributory and done with cheerfulness, even with chronic and consistent pain. I will seek to grow in Christ from a faulty and bloated perspective of my faith. Let’s use the Corinthian church as an example. The brethren there had a lot of issues, and one of them was spiritual pride, bragging about who they were following—Paul, Apollos or Peter.

Paul is being sarcastic here:

1 Corinthians 4:8–10: 8 You are already filled, you have already become rich, you have become kings without us; and indeed, I wish that you had become kings so that we also might reign with you. 9 For, I think, God has exhibited us apostles last of all, as men condemned to death; because we have become a spectacle to the world, both to angels and to men. 10 We are fools for Christ's sake, but you are prudent in Christ; we are weak, but you are strong; you are distinguished, but we are without honor.

Verse 10: (NLT) Our dedication to Christ makes us look like fools, but you claim to be so wise in Christ! We are weak, but you are so powerful! You are honored, but we are ridiculed. The attitude of the Corinthians wasn’t going to bring growth and change.

Romans 6:16: Do you not know that when you present yourselves to someone as slaves for obedience, you are slaves of the one whom you obey, either of sin resulting in death, or of obedience resulting in righteousness?

We just did two episodes about being biased. Our natural inclinations often lead us in the opposite direction of God’s ways. Biases bring change distortions because they influence how we view things. Reality asks the brutally difficult question, “What am I a slave to?” We are all slaves to something. Let’s not try to make ourselves look pretty like the Corinthians did. We need to recognize where we are trapped so we can break free. Either way, whether it is abandonment of sinful ways or alteration we need to be working on, let me be steeped in reality, for that is where the Lord’s hand can most easily reach me.

Let’s circle back to our episode title. How much change is enough? Can it EVER be enough if we are trying to have a Christlike character?

No, but we can’t look at that through the eyes of discouragement. We must look at it through the eyes of blessing. Spiritual change is always a blessing from God. So, let’s rephrase that question: Can God’s blessings EVER be enough? No! Let’s look at our spiritual changes through those precise eyes.

Sometimes we take the act of recognizing a problem for granted. We need to be sure that our recognition is based on truth—God’s truth!

So, we are pursuing strong and productive change.

What follows our desire to change and our recognition of our issues? Taking these two steps is enormous progress if we take them with sincerity and honesty. The next step is logical. We need a plan—a method of attack—to undo that which is not beneficial. We cannot stress enough that merely undoing something must always be followed by filling the gap that it leaves. Without this replacement, any change we seek will simply fizzle away.

CHANGE PROCEEDS WITH PLANNING. Intentional direction inevitably works better than emotional imagination and human desire.

That sounds like the “happily ever after” syndrome, fueled by seeing everyone else’s manufactured perfection on social media.

Let us be driven by reality as we intentionally seek real change:

Romans 12:4: For just as we have many members in one body and all the members do not have the same function,… We are unique. We can’t be compared to (or compare ourselves to) others.

Whether we are altering or abandoning something, our intention is revealed in our true desires:

1 Peter 2:1-2: 1 Therefore, putting aside all malice and all deceit and hypocrisy and envy and all slander.

Wow, that’s a big list to put aside, covering a wide range of our natural, human tendencies! 2 like newborn babies, long for (intensely crave) the pure milk of the word, so that by it you may grow in respect to salvation.

Our intensity for God’s word should be like the intensity of a newborn infant craving the milk from their mother. All a newborn knows is hunger. If we are basking in our malice, deceit and hypocrisy, we don’t have room for a hunger for the word of God. We are too busy with other things. Clean house! Make room in our spiritual home for our spiritual lives, and then we will crave the pure milk of the word.

Practical advice—watch out for the company you keep:

Proverbs 13:20: (NLT) Walk with the wise and become wise; associate with fools and get in trouble.

This applies at any age, young or old, virtual or in real life.

When we are looking to make real change, we must put a plan in place. With a difficult challenge like an addiction, we have to find the patterns that create the addictive behavior. When we identify them, we change them. If we know walking past a bar will tempt us to enter, we don’t think, Next time I walk past I won’t go in. The next time, we must go completely out of the way to avoid going anywhere near the bar! This is how we put a plan in place.

I follow Jesus, so I should be able to have what I want.

Let’s look at this example in Mark:

Mark 10:35,37: 35 James and John, the two sons of Zebedee, came up to Jesus, saying, Teacher, we want you to do for us whatever we ask of you. 37 They said to him, Grant that we may sit, one on your right and one on your left, in your glory.

Do for us whatever we ask of you—this was a bold ask! Today we hear this in the form of “decree and declare” or “name it and claim it” where people demand the holy spirit—God’s power and influence—do something for them like make them rich, find their lost keys or bring them a spouse.

This request showed a lack of maturity as our imaginations and human desires can hijack our change.

The request from James and John showed a simple lack of maturity. (The “decree and declare,” or “name it and claim it” shows a brashness that goes against the humility we are supposed to have, as shown throughout the New Testament.) James and John had a more childlike lack of maturity. Their imagination and human desires hijacked their work on changing themselves and following Jesus. This distorted their reality. When this happens, we get lost. They did not have the teachings of the New Testament yet and were probably just wanting to be with their beloved Lord.

Jesus condescended to wash the apostles’ feet. He condescended to die in an unlawful crucifixion, to give his life for ours. Let us condescend to THAT kind of attitude. What does Jesus do with this bold ask by James and John? He handled this childish request with grace and love:

Mark 10:38–40: 38 But Jesus said to them, You do not know what you are asking. Are you able to drink the cup that I drink, or to be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized?

39 They said to him, We are able. And Jesus said to them, The cup that I drink you shall drink; and you shall be baptized with the baptism with which I am baptized. 40 But to sit on my right or on my left, this is not mine to give; but it is for those for whom it has been prepared. The answer from Jesus was not what they asked for; it was better. His answer was, You are going to experience things I experience. You will grow up, mature and learn to be like me. You will live a life of sacrifice by doing God's will and not your own. They would become spiritually mature, and it would fundamentally change who they were. This change in them would bless others. This is a better outcome! It is a good idea to write down our plan to help to seal our intentions:

Habakkuk 2:2: Then the LORD answered me and said, Record the vision and inscribe it on tablets, that the one who reads it may run. (Source: Forbes Magazine, Neuroscience Explains Why You Need to Write Down Your Goals If You Actually Want to Achieve Them, by Mark Murphy) “Vividly describing your goals in written form is strongly associated with goal success, and people who very vividly describe or picture their goals are anywhere from 1.2 to 1.4 times more likely to successfully accomplish their goals than people who don’t.”

The article goes on to say when you write something down, not only do you have a visual reminder in front of you, but it helps with encoding, where the brain decides what gets stored in long-term memory. In addition, memory improves when you are the one physically doing the writing, rather than just reading from a source. Writing our goals down is a good, practical way to look at them and check our progress. We want to put a plan in place to help us understand the fundamental issues we are working towards. To “decree and declare” walks away from God’s providence because that is not a scriptural approach. We can’t allow anything to distort our plan. We have to be working in reality— in an intentional direction based on God’s word. His word helps us plan. CHANGE GROWS WITH ACCOUNTABILITY. Let’s drive our accountability by acknowledging excellence—something high and lofty we can look up to.

Romans 12:9–13: 9 Let love (agape or selfless love) be without hypocrisy. Abhor what is evil; cling to what is good. 10 Be devoted to one another in brotherly love; give preference to one another in honor; 11 not lagging behind in diligence, fervent in spirit, serving the Lord; 12 rejoicing in hope, persevering in tribulation, devoted to prayer, 13 contributing to the needs of the saints, practicing hospitality.

This scripture made me think of my New Year’s resolution—I want each day to be “purposeful.” I want to let each day begin ready to do God’s will with my words, my thoughts and my actions. This automatically takes distortions or things of no value and pushes them away. I want to ask each morning, what can I do to bless others?

That’s interesting because in the last episode, #1316, I talked about the word that keeps following me—“irrelevant”—as I see what other people are doing. I want to focus just on how I am supposed to think, speak and act. What others do is irrelevant if they are doing something wrong.

“Purposeful” and “irrelevant” sound like opposites, but they actually work precisely together because to be purposeful in Christlikeness is to make the world around us irrelevant. It is the same thing from different sides. These are motivators when used appropriately.

I know I’m accountable, but… In the Parable of the Talents, the master gives each of his servants a large sum of money to work with while he’s away.

He comes back and rewards those who multiplied the money, but the one who did nothing with it makes excuses:

Matthew 25:24–25: 24 And the one also who had received the one talent came up and said, Master, I knew you to be a hard man, reaping where you did not sow and gathering where you scattered no seed. 25 And I was afraid, and went away and hid your talent in the ground. See, you have what is yours.

He had the same accountability as the other servants but didn’t want to do the work. He blamed his boss for why he buried the talent he was given. We don’t want to put our responsibilities on someone else. We certainly don’t want to have a bunch of excuses for God and Jesus when they ask why we didn’t strive to change.

Realistically, our desire to change can be thwarted by any number of excuses, including procrastination, surrendering because it’s just too difficult, or even stalling by having to keep gathering information before actually doing anything about the problem.

(Source: John Maxwell Maximum Impact Series lesson called, “Making good decisions better”) The Power of Procrastination: Procrastination is often disguised as rational thinking. It ends up a welcome response when disguised this way because it feeds our desire for inaction and seems to give us great reasons for doing nothing… The Slippery Slope of Surrendering: When a decision is exceptionally difficult, it can cause us to cave in, as we have been depleted of so much energy that we lose our will to fight. The Inaction of Information Gathering: The “necessity” of gathering an ever-larger pile of information before actually deciding to do something about it.

Accountability implies action and doing. We need to be doing!

Luke 19 tells the story of Zaccheus, an unpopular tax collector working for the Roman government. He went to great lengths to see Jesus, who acknowledged him and stayed at his house.

Zaccheus was so overjoyed:

Luke 19:8–9: 8 Zaccheus stopped and said to the Lord, Behold, Lord, half of my possessions I will give to the poor, and if I have defrauded anyone of anything, I will give back four times as much. 9 And Jesus said to him, Today salvation has come to this house, because he, too, is a son of Abraham.

No one demanded that Zaccheus give any money back. But he demonstrated the change he experienced in following Jesus by giving back half of what he legitimately earned and four times what he got by cheating the people. What a beautiful example of making things right!

He made his past right so that his future could be opened to the joy of following Jesus. This is something we all need to think about. This is a changed reality when it comes to accountability.

We don’t want to tell anybody else of our failings, but an extra level of accountability is a great motivator.

We need to find the right kind of person we can really lean on to be encouraging, even if we fall down. Accountability will drive us toward successful change in Christ. Accountability is really hard for most of us. What if we don’t do what we said we would do? Well, that’s the whole point of being accountable! Don’t lose that. So far, we have put all of the work steps in place for the changes we seek to spiritually achieve. Where do we go from here?

Having these steps in place is crucial to our making change real and lasting. What comes next can be summed up in one simple phrase: persistent effort and dogged determination. Once we put the process in place, we simply need to follow through again and again and again and again...

Successful change in Christ is a fruitful and fulfilling journey.

CHANGE MATURES WITH NEW HABITS. Let us continually drive these new habits forward by focusing on how they bring us closer to the selfless dedication we need to follow Christ.

Change can grow with accountability, but it matures as we practice our new habits.

Romans 12:14–18: 14 Bless those who persecute you; bless and do not curse. (That’s selflessness!) 15 Rejoice with those who rejoice, and weep with those who weep. (That’s selflessness!) 16 Be of the same mind toward one another; do not be haughty in mind, but associate with the lowly. (That’s selflessness!) Do not be wise in your own estimation. (That’s selflessness!) 17 Never pay back evil for evil to anyone. Respect what is right in the sight of all men. (That’s definitely selflessness!) 18 If possible, so far as it depends on you, be at peace with all men. (That’s selflessness!)

Do you see the theme here? SELFLESSNESS! This describes the selfless character of Christ and is the level we want to reach.

Selflessness is written all over the New Testament. Our change can mature with selfless dedication. What could distort this path towards change maturing with new habits? I try, but I am not as strong as God wants me to be. I just can’t do it. It is so easy to take a small statement of Scripture and flash it as “proof” of our unworthy feelings:

Romans 3:23: for all have sinned and fall short of the glory of God.

I am unworthy!

Isaiah 64:6: For all of us have become like one who is unclean, and all our righteous deeds are like a filthy garment; and all of us wither like a leaf, and our iniquities, like the wind, take us away.

I am too far gone before God and should just disappear!

This distortion is insidious, even in those with great spiritual growth and maturity and a strong track record of service. They don’t rise up to the next level. Satan wins in this kind of distortion.

Of course we are not worthy. That’s what being covered by the robe of Christ’s righteousness is all about. Not being worthy means we have an opportunity to grow and learn.

It comes back to the Apostle Paul boasting about his weaknesses because that is what Christ’s strength replaces. That is what brings him up and makes him change and grow, and understand and empathize with the weaknesses of others. We must not get stuck in the distortion that we cannot measure up. God would not have called us if that was the case.

Romans 8:28: And we know that God causes all things to work together for good to those who love God, to those who are called according to His purpose.

We make the effort, and God blesses the effort as He sees fit. What I consider “success” likely isn’t God’s definition. And what I consider “failure” is likely not God’s definition either. God sees the effort, and He sees our heart. We tend to overlook those things, but we have to rely on our heavenly Father—He would not give a promise like Romans 8:28 if He wasn’t serious!

God is committed to our spiritual changes and WILL back His commitment:

Romans 8:31–35: 31 …If God is for us, who is against us? 32 He who did not spare His own son, but delivered him over for us all, how will He not also with him freely give us all things? 33 Who will bring a charge against God's elect? God is the one who justifies; 34 who is the one who condemns? Christ Jesus is he who died, yes, rather who was raised, who is at the right hand of God, who also intercedes for us. 35 Who will separate us from the love of Christ? Will tribulation, or distress, or persecution, or famine, or nakedness, or peril, or sword?

We can see the power of God’s commitment here.

But notice Paul writes, Christ Jesus is he who died…but also, who was raised, who is at the right hand of God. Because Christ is right next to the Father, he intercedes for us. God is committed to us and to this process. This is the change reality we can rely on!

Jesus knows what it is like to be human. This is the beauty of the reality of our change in maturing as we develop these new habits.

When we abandon our old earthly habits, it changes our lives. When we alter our habits to live to a higher standard, it crystallizes our characters. We can see how the two work together. The changes in our lives mature with the practicing of our new habits. CHANGE BECOMES REALITY WITH TIME. Focusing with simplicity and clarity drives these new habits into being.

Romans 12:21: Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good.

This verse sums up all that we have looked at today, because through the strength of God through Christ, do not be overcome with evil. This takes away all the excuses and distortions. We can overcome evil with good. This is the reality we want to live in Christ! Be aware, however, change becoming a reality with time can be distorted. I have worked, and I have attained. I have done well, and I can rest. This speaks to our title’s question about how much change is enough. Are we ever done? The third chapter of Revelation uses seven literal churches established by the apostles to symbolically describe the condition of Jesus’ followers throughout the entire age of the gospel message being proclaimed. Each church represents a time period and a message for that stage of the gospel church. The message to the last church, the church of Laodicea, corresponds to our time.

Revelation 3:15–19 15 I know your deeds, that you are neither cold nor hot; I wish that you were cold or hot (this refers to the spiritual condition and the danger of complacency). 16 So because you are lukewarm, and neither hot nor cold, I will spit you out of my mouth. 17 Because you say, I am rich, and have become wealthy, and have need of nothing, and you do not know that you are wretched and miserable and poor and blind and naked, 18 I advise you to buy from me gold refined by fire so that you may become rich, and white garments so that you may clothe yourself, and that the shame of your nakedness will not be revealed; and eye salve to anoint your eyes so that you may see. 19 Those whom I love, I reprove and discipline; therefore be zealous and repent.

The distortion here is the comfortability of having arrived. We think about how we used to be and see some improvement. We become complacent about our lives. We need instead to think about how well others can now see Christ in us. We can’t sit back and relax. Complacency is the enemy of true spiritual change. It is a distortion of thinking that the change we have made is sufficient.

Should we ever be complacent? No, of course not! There is always room for growth. The Pharisees had the attitude that no one except them was good enough. Only they were right with God—we should never go there!

To be complacent is to turn our back on God and Jesus.

Paul speaks of his life-long challenge:

Philippians 3:13–14: 13 Brethren, I do not regard myself as having laid hold of it yet; but one thing I do: forgetting what lies behind and reaching forward to what lies ahead, 14 I press on toward the goal for the prize of the upward call of God in Christ Jesus.

Paul is saying, I will not stop. There is a great blessing in this because we should always be extending ourselves a little further.

In my own life, I learn the most when I get extended beyond where I used to be. By pushing further, I learn something new, something greater in the service of our heavenly Father. The challenge is always going to be there. Along with the challenge, the blessing is also always going to be there!

Blessing:

Romans 8:37–39: 37 But in all these things we overwhelmingly conquer through Him who loved us. 38 For I am convinced that neither death, nor life, nor angels, nor principalities, nor things present, nor things to come, nor powers, 39 nor height, nor depth, nor any other created thing, will be able to separate us from the love of God, which is in Christ Jesus our Lord. Here is a list of what can’t touch us when we engage in spiritual change, understanding the distortions and holding onto the realities. The one thing not on that list is ME. I can reverse all of that. I can open the door for Satan to go to work on things in my life. If we keep the challenge in front of us, we will keep the blessings at hand.

If God called us, we are worthy. Let’s work towards that worthiness. God doesn’t look at us through rose-colored glasses. He sees Jesus’ blood-stained sacrifice which covers us. He’s not making light of our weaknesses. He wants us melded and worked into something that becomes glorious.

This is an amazing offer given to every single “called” Christian. If we are called to follow Christ and are given God’s spirit, this is the offer. Change becomes a critical part of how we get to something that becomes glorious. We can’t get there by staying where we began. We need to take the steps, put away the distortions and hold onto the realities that step- by-step help us to abandon those things that need to be abandoned, and alter those things that need to be altered.

We need to rise up to a level where God can use us in a way we never thought possible. It can happen if we rely on the word of God and Christ as our advocate. So, it’s time to change but how much is enough?

For Rick, Jonathan, Julie and Christian Questions… …

## Episode 811 — What About Divorce?
Published: 2014-04-27
Episode page: https://christianquestions.com/society/811-what-about-divorce/

Genesis 2:24: (NKJV) Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and be joined to his wife, and they shall become one flesh.

As Christians, we all have a sense of the sanctity of marriage. We all know that it is supposed to be ‘til death do us part, yet we also experience about as high a rate of divorce as the rest of our society. Does Jesus give us solid guidelines for marriage and divorce? Should Christians be involved in “no fault” divorces? Do you really have to stay married even if you are not happy? Stay with us as we look into this difficult, sensitive and very relevant matter!

On this program we will discuss a very high standard intended towards Christians. That is not to say the principles are not good for everyone else. If you are a Christian and espouse the teachings of Jesus and the Apostles, then these principles apply to you.

Let’s set the basis for getting our minds right about the whole marriage arrangement:

Genesis 2:21-24: (KJV) 21And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof; 22And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man. 23And Adam said, this is now bone of my bones, and flesh of my flesh: she shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. 24Therefore shall a man leave his father and his mother, and shall cleave unto his wife: and they shall be one flesh.

Why did God take a rib? Perhaps because it is close to the man’s heart and is protected by his arms. It shows a closeness by which a husband and wife should be operating.

God invented this relationship of marriage with at least two purposes:

1) companionship and 2) procreation. In the marriage arrangement God invented, the children are protected by a mother and a father. Children are educated as they are nurtured and grow.

Divorce reasons changed, The Impact of Divorce on Children, Tamara D. Afifi, TED talk - Divorce is common. It’s less stigmatized. So, why would the differences between children of divorced and non-divorced families be increasing? One of Palamato’s (a sociologist and mentor of the speaker) suggestions was: well, maybe it’s because the reasons for divorce are different than they used to be. When people got divorced in the 1970’s, it’s because it’s a really bad marriage, right? You know, adultery, all these other things, and they really needed to get out of it. Today people are getting divorced for personal happiness and that could really bother children, right? That’s not enough. People are getting divorced too easily.

Marriage is the highest and most sacred relationship that God ever gave to man.

It is so valuable and so sacred, that God saw fit to seal this relationship with a covenant made in His presence:

Matthew 19:6: (KJV) So that they are no more two, but one flesh. What therefore God hath joined together, let not man put asunder.

What is God’s opinion on divorce?

The following text refers to the sons of Judah, specifically the priests abandoning their Hebrew wives in favor of other foreign and idolatrous women:

Malachi 2:11-16: (ASV) 11Judah hath dealt treacherously, and an abomination is committed in Israel… for Judah hath profaned the holiness of Jehovah which he loveth, and hath married the daughter of a foreign god… 13And this again ye do: ye cover the altar of Jehovah with tears, with weeping, and with sighing, insomuch that he regardeth not the offering any more, neither receiveth it with good will at your hand. 14Yet ye say, Wherefore? Because Jehovah hath been witness between thee and the wife of thy youth, against whom thou hast dealt treacherously, though she is thy companion, and the wife of thy covenant. 15And did he not make one, although he had the residue of the Spirit? And wherefore one? He sought a godly seed. Therefore take heed to your spirit, and let none deal treacherously against the wife of his youth. 16For I hate putting away (Revised Standard Version: “I hate divorce.”), saith Jehovah, the God of Israel, and him that covereth his garment with violence, saith Jehovah of hosts: therefore take heed to your spirit that ye deal not treacherously.

It is very important as Christians that when we read through the Scriptures, we try to get God’s mind on things. We are told that God’s ways are higher than our ways, so we have to struggle a bit, but God has a reason for everything He does. The closer we get to His attitude, the more we will understand what those reasons are.

From Good Parenting Institute, found on letsloop.com. Ryan Harris is a life coach… Set an example, Coping With the Emotional Impact of Marriage, Ryan Harris (life coach), Good Parenting Institute, letsloop.com

- So, the first thing is, before my ex-wife and I decided to get a divorce, I was grappling with the biggest thing: how is it going to affect our child, (in your case, maybe “children”) and the thing that I kept coming back to use as a thing to sort of rely on, I as a father wanted to set a fantastic example for my child. Marriage is a “Covenant of God,” therefore the marriage covenant has three parties involved. (Source: McClintock and Strong’s Cyclopedia) COVENANT OF GOD: Properly, of a covenant between man and man; i.e. a solemn compact or agreement, either between tribes or nations (1 Samuel 11:1; Joshua 9:6,15), or between individuals (Genesis 21:44), by which each party bound himself to fulfill certain conditions, and was assured of receiving certain advantages. In making such a covenant God was solemnly invoked as witness (Genesis 31:50), whence the expression “a covenant of Jehovah,” 1 Samuel 20:8; compare Jeremiah 34:18, 19; Ezekiel 17:19), and an oath was sworn (Genesis 21:31); and accordingly a breach of covenant was regarded as a very heinous sin (Ezekiel 17:12-20).

Theoretically, recognition of God in a marriage arrangement would strengthen that relationship. It should be a factor against divorce.

Whenever there is conflict in a marriage – and there inevitably will be disagreements – both the husband and wife should remember God was a witness as part of that covenant. It should allow them to be able to resolve that conflict in a way that pleases Him. God is part of that relationship. Statistically, however, the Christian nations have as high a divorce rate as everybody else. That tells us something is wrong somewhere!

The example, Coping With the Emotional Impact of Marriage, Ryan Harris (life coach), Good Parenting Institute, letsloop.com

- Then I thought to myself, would I want my son to settle for a relationship that was less than ideal with a partner that was not an appropriate match and just struggle it out because people say you shouldn’t get divorced? Or would I set a good example for my son and say, look, you can have whatever you want! Go for it! You can be happy, no matter what. Just go for it and don’t settle. So, no disrespect to my ex-wife, of course, she is a fantastic person, one of the best teachers I have ever met. What gave me the courage to finally proceed with the divorce was the idea of I wanted to set, as a man, as a father, I wanted to set as good an example that I could for my son. So, that’s a big one. I did not want my son to see me in a relationship that was not ideal. What example is it to tell a child that we have to do what is pleasing to us? It is the ultimate example of selfishness. This does not match biblical principles. If we are Christians in covenant relationship with God, we have to ask if that kind of thinking appeals to us. If it does, we have to question the basis of our Christianity, which is about something bigger and higher. The essence of Christianity is sacrifice – giving up your own preferences and comforts so as to do the will of God and be of service to others. That principle works very well in creating a strong marriage bond – giving up what you want so that your partner can have what they want.

How did the Old Testament Law define divorce?

Old Testament definition of divorce:

Deuteronomy 24:1-4: (ASV) 1When a man taketh a wife, and marrieth her, then it shall be, if she find no favor in his eyes, because he hath found some unseemly thing in her, that he shall write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house. 2And when she is departed out of his house, she may go and be another man’s wife. 3And if the latter husband hate her, and write her a bill of divorcement, and give it in her hand, and send her out of his house; or if the latter husband die, who took her to be his wife; 4her former husband, who sent her away, may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled; for that is abomination before Jehovah: and thou shalt not cause the land to sin, which Jehovah thy God giveth thee for an inheritance.

Here are five points of clarity on the above text to affirm it is teaching that divorce is a complete loosing from and breaking of the marriage contract:

1. He shall write her a bill of divorcement: He writes the contract, affirming the dissolving of the covenant in writing which shows its legality and permanence.

2. Give it in her hand: This phrase is extremely common in the Old Testament and can depict a giving over of power, responsibility and control. The woman having this written document in her hand signifies she, not her former husband, has complete power over her life. She has the legal right in her hand to leave.

3. Send her out of his house: The contract has been broken in writing; she has its authority in her own hand and now she is sent out of her house.

4. There is a former husband and a latter husband – both are considered husbands on an equal basis. After receiving a bill of divorcement, she was permitted to enter into a marriage covenant with a second or latter husband.

5. There is potential for defilement and abomination. This sin could happen only if the divorced and remarried woman would be, under any circumstances, reunited to the first husband - may not take her again to be his wife, after that she is defiled. “Merry go round marriages” were not permitted.

Jeremiah 3:1: (NRSV) If a man divorces his wife and she goes from him and becomes another man’s wife, will he return to her? Would not such a land be greatly polluted? You have played the whore with many lovers; and would you return to me? Says the LORD.

In the New Testament, adultery is a key part of divorce. In the Old Testament, adultery and fornication are not mentioned, rather, an unseemly thing. They are not mentioned because under the Law the penalty was not simply divorce but a death penalty for such sexual immorality.

Observation Point: Thus far, the Law seems clear: Marriage is sacred. Yet for the hardness of man’s imperfect hearts, God in the Old Testament did allow divorce and that allowance was a clearly stated and unequivocal dissolution of the marriage covenant.

Unseemly is used as a reason for divorce. What does this mean? (Source: Samuele Bacchiocchi, PhD., Andrews University) The Hebrew word erwath (generally translated, "indecency" or "uncleanness") is often used to refer to shameful exposure of the human body (Genesis 9:22,23; Exodus 20:26; Lamentations 1:8; Ezekiel 16:36,37). In

Deuteronomy 23:13-14, the word is used to describe the failure to cover human excrement. We would conclude, then, that according to Deuteronomy 24:1, divorce was allowed for some kind of shameful act or indecency other than illicit sexual intercourse.

God often allows things that are not necessarily what He wants. There is God’s intentional will and permissive will. God allows divorce, but His intention for our ideal spirituality would be to have marriage for life. God will tolerate some things and can potentially bless us in spite of what we do vs. God blessing what we do because we are following His will.

Two examples of this:

1. Kings in ancient Israel: God did not want Israel to have kings but God permitted it with all of the problems that went along with a king.

2. God’s permission of evil in this world: Some people believe that God’s permission of evil means He does not care. That is a mistake. Evil is permitted for a time and for a purpose.

AAALLLW W WAAAYYYSSS LLLO OOO OOKKK FFFO OORRR G GGO OODDD’’’SSS IIIN NNTTTEEEN NNTTTIIIO OON NNAAALLL W W WIIILLLLLL AAAN NNDDD N NNO OOTTT H HHIIISSS PPPEEERRRM MMIIISSSSSSIIIVVVEEE W W WIIILLLLLL...

We don’t want to be a “bottom feeder Christian,” getting along with just the bare minimum of what God will tolerate. We are supposed to walk in the footsteps of Jesus. Marriage and divorce are subjects of hard-hitting truths to understand.

Not a coward, Coping With the Emotional Impact of Marriage, Ryan Harris (life coach), Good Parenting Institute, letsloop.com

- Now, you can make any relationship ideal through energy, work, proper focus, appreciating the heck out of your partner to make almost any situation turn around. But I felt that this was not the appropriate partner after seven and a half years for me, and I just thought I don’t want to set the example of being someone who’s cowardly, who settles, who doesn’t go for their dreams; I wouldn’t want to display that for my son. So, that was the biggest - that’s probably number one - not to get divorced, but the thing that helped me feel comfortable with the idea of actually proceeding with the divorce, because I just wanted to be a good role model for my son, and I thought actually proceeding with the divorce was setting a better example than staying in the marriage.

This is so contrary to Scripture and a good Christian marriage. The audio example has no interest in resolving issues. If you have made a commitment and are so easily willing to walk away from such a commitment, you are a coward! Fight for commitment’s sake!

Dependability is another important aspect of this. Pursuing your own selfish goals makes you undependable. What kind of example is that to the child? So, what did Jesus have to say about divorce?

Matthew 5:27-32: (KJV) 27Ye have heard that it was said by them of old time, Thou shalt not commit adultery: 28But I say unto you, that whosoever looketh on a woman to lust after her hath committed adultery with her already in his heart. 29And if thy right eye offend thee, pluck it out, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell. (Gehenna) 30And if thy right hand offend thee, cut it off, and cast it from thee: for it is profitable for thee that one of thy members should perish, and not that thy whole body should be cast into hell. (Gehenna) 31It hath been said, Whosoever shall put away his wife, let him give her a writing of divorcement: 32But I say unto you, That whosoever shall put away his wife, saving for the cause of fornication, causeth her to commit adultery: and whosoever shall marry her that is divorced committeth adultery.

Jesus raised the standard as high as possible! He is telling us not to do the things that will be offensive to God; do not even THINK those things! Assess yourself.

This presents a major change from the Old Testament! He wanted the original standard of ONE MAN + ONE WOMAN = ONE LIFE. There is no reason or legitimate cause for divorce except sexual immorality. That was a big change from the legalistic thinking of the Jews at that time.

Jesus designates his audience and to whom this new standard applies:

Matthew 19:11: (ASV) But he said unto them, not all men can receive this saying (those outside of the Christian world), but they to whom it is given.

Jesus wanted the highest quality of disciple, so a high standard was necessary. A caller suggests: Marriage is by divine design. Jesus and his bride are the model for marriage. Man has a propensity to dilute and corrupt God’s beautiful designs and illustrations. Trouble arises when we deviate from God’s law. Statistics, Effects of Divorce on Children, Marriage Resource Center of Miami Valley - Statistically, children are profoundly affected. One third of all children are born out of wedlock and thirty-five million children have seen their parents divorce since 1970. They’re five times more likely to live in poverty than those in intact homes and three times more apt to be expelled from school and twelve times more likely to be jailed. Nationally only 45 percent of teenagers live with their married mother and father.

How sad! Godly principles of love, being respectful and doing justice to each other will help us to avoid a lot of this. The more we apply these standards in our lives, the fewer problems we will have.

Did the Apostle’s teachings support those of Jesus?

A caller suggests: What about separation? What about in the case of mental or physical abuse?

There are situations that are truly intolerable, such as when a spouse’s life is threatened. Situations arise where it is a sad but prudent thing to separate.
